headline: Eradicated in 1980
detail: A disease that killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone. The last natural case was in Somalia in October 1977, and the World Health Assembly certified it eradicated in May 1980.
how: Every country had to finish the job, because one country with smallpox left all the others at risk. That gave each a reason to take part, as long as it trusted the rest to do the same (Barrett, 2016).
source_name: Our World in Data, Smallpox (citing D. A. Henderson)

headline: Nearly 99% of ozone-harming chemicals phased out
detail: Recovery to 1980 levels is projected around 2040 for most of the world, 2045 over the Arctic and 2066 over the Antarctic, if current policies stay in place.
how: The Montreal Protocol (1987) did more than ask for cuts: it banned trade in the chemicals with countries outside the treaty, which made joining every country's own best choice (Barrett, 2016).
source_name: UN News, reporting the Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion 2022

headline: Gone from every country since 2021
detail: More than 100 countries still sold it when the UN campaign began in 2002. Algeria, the last, ran out in July 2021. UNEP estimates the ban prevents more than 1.2 million premature deaths a year (modelled).
how: A 19-year UN-led partnership of governments, fuel companies and civil society worked country by country until none was left.
source_name: UN Environment Programme, press release 30 Aug 2021 (via Al Jazeera)

headline: Wild polio cases down more than 99% since 1988
detail: From an estimated 350,000 cases a year in more than 125 countries to two countries where it still spreads, Afghanistan and Pakistan.
how: Like smallpox, it only ends when the last country finishes, and the last strongholds are the hardest (Barrett).
source_name: World Health Organization, Poliomyelitis fact sheet

headline: Down from about 70,300 warheads to about 12,187
how: Most of the cuts came after the Cold War. The job is not finished: the number of warheads ready for military use is rising again.
source_name: Federation of American Scientists, Status of World Nuclear Forces, 2026
